items.stem: State what is meant by the term "edge (graph)".
items.answer: A stored, named relationship between two nodes in a graph database, such as FRIEND_OF

items.stem: Distinguish between a relational database and a graph database.
items.answer: A graph database stores relationships explicitly as edges and traverses them directly; a relational database represents relationships with foreign keys and reconstructs them with joins.
items.markingKey: A graph database stores relationships explicitly as edges and traverses them directly; a relational database represents relationships with foreign keys and reconstructs them with joins. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why graph databases outperform relational databases for deep relationship queries.
items.answer: Edges are stored with each node (index-free adjacency), so each hop is a pointer traversal; a relational database needs a join per hop, whose cost grows with table size and depth.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Edges are stored with each node (index-free adjacency), so each hop is a pointer traversal; a relational database needs a join per hop, whose cost grows with table size and depth. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
A key-value database is used as a session cache for a game server in Singapore. It starts empty. PUT k v stores v under k (overwriting), INCR k adds 1 (treating a missing key as 0), DELETE k removes k, and GET k returns the value or nil. Trace these operations and give the value returned by each GET and the final contents:
PUT sess:b7 1
PUT sess:b7 2
PUT cart:9 2
INCR sess:b7
INCR sess:b7
GET flag:dark
GET cart:9
items.answer: GET results: flag:dark → nil; cart:9 → 2. Final store: cart:9=2, sess:b7=4.
items.markingKey: GET results: flag:dark → nil; cart:9 → 2. Final store: cart:9=2, sess:b7=4. 1 mark per correct GET (max 3), 1 mark final store.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that a document database is the best choice for an e-commerce platform.
items.answer: A document store suits the catalogue; payments and inventory are better kept in a relational, ACID-compliant database – a polyglot design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: product data varies by category; orders can be stored as single documents; scales horizontally for traffic peaks. Arguments against: payments and stock need strong consistency across documents; reporting across customers and products needs joins; duplicated embedded data may become inconsistent. Supported judgement: A document store suits the catalogue; payments and inventory are better kept in a relational, ACID-compliant database – a polyglot design.

items.stem: Explain why key-value stores are very fast.
items.answer: Each value is located directly by hashing its key, with no query parsing, joins or schema checks; data is often held in memory and spread across nodes by key.

items.answer: Embedding often duplicates data (e.g. customer address copied into each order document) which can become inconsistent; designers trade duplication for read speed.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Building a data warehouse is worthwhile for a medium-sized retail chain.
items.answer: Usually worthwhile once data from several systems must be analysed regularly; cloud warehouses reduce cost, but benefits depend on data quality and clear business questions.

items.stem:
(a) Kenji writes: "Replicating data on more nodes always makes the database more consistent." Explain why this is inaccurate. [2]
(b) A distributed key-value store replicates every item on N = 5 nodes. A write succeeds after W = 3 nodes confirm it and a read queries R = 4 nodes. Determine whether every read is guaranteed to return the most recent write. [3]
(c) Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that a global e-commerce company should use a distributed rather than a centralised database. [4]
items.answer: (a) More replicas improve availability but make it harder to keep every copy identical; consistency needs synchronous or quorum writes. (b) R + W = 7 > N = 5, so reads are guaranteed to see the latest write (strong consistency). (c) For a global company the availability and latency benefits usually outweigh the complexity, provided critical transactions use strong consistency.

(c) [4 marks] Arguments for: lower latency for users worldwide; no single point of failure; scales by adding nodes; supports regional data-protection laws. Arguments against: more complex to design and administer; consistency across sites is harder (CAP trade-offs); distributed transactions are slower; higher network and security costs. items.stem: A distributed database for a bank in Seoul partitions customer records across 3 nodes (0–2) using node = CustomerID mod 3. State the node for each CustomerID: 6647, 2107, 9958, 4457, 3378, 5330, 9620, 6922. A node is then added (node = CustomerID mod 4). How many of these records must move?
items.answer: 6647 → node 2; 2107 → node 1; 9958 → node 1; 4457 → node 2; 3378 → node 0; 5330 → node 2; 9620 → node 2; 6922 → node 1. After adding a node, 7 of 8 records move.
items.markingKey: 6647 → node 2; 2107 → node 1; 9958 → node 1; 4457 → node 2; 3378 → node 0; 5330 → node 2; 9620 → node 2; 6922 → node 1. After adding a node, 7 of 8 records move. This shows why simple modulo hashing is costly to re-partition; consistent hashing moves far fewer keys. 1 mark per two correct placements.

items.stem:
(a) Define the term "temporal database". [2]
(b) Explain the difference between raster spatial data and vector spatial data. [2]
(c) Sofia writes: "Temporal databases simply add a timestamp column showing when a row was last changed." Explain why this is inaccurate. [3]
items.answer: (a) A database that records time periods for which facts are valid (valid time) and/or when they were stored (transaction time), keeping history (b) Raster data is a grid of cells (pixels) such as satellite images; vector data uses points, lines and polygons such as roads and boundaries. (c) They store periods of validity for every version, keeping full history, not only the last update time.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A document database is the best choice for an e-commerce platform."
items.answer: A document store suits the catalogue; payments and inventory are better kept in a relational, ACID-compliant database – a polyglot design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: product data varies by category; orders can be stored as single documents; scales horizontally for traffic peaks. Arguments against: payments and stock need strong consistency across documents; reporting across customers and products needs joins; duplicated embedded data may become inconsistent. Supported judgement: A document store suits the catalogue; payments and inventory are better kept in a relational, ACID-compliant database – a polyglot design.

Case study context: Aurora Energy, a utility in Toronto, collects smart-meter readings in a distributed database, detects faults with anomaly detection and models its devices as objects in a simulation.
(a) Mei writes: "OLAP cubes can only have three dimensions." Explain why this is inaccurate. Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [2]
(b) To what extent is it true that Building a data warehouse is worthwhile for a medium-sized retail chain? Refer to Aurora Energy in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) A "cube" can have any number of dimensions (hypercube); three is just easy to draw. (b) Usually worthwhile once data from several systems must be analysed regularly; cloud warehouses reduce cost, but benefits depend on data quality and clear business questions.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] A "cube" can have any number of dimensions (hypercube); three is just easy to draw. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: integrated historical data supports trend analysis and forecasting; OLAP lets managers analyse by region/product/time; removes analytical load from the till system. Arguments against: high cost of design, ETL development and storage; data is only as current as the last load; requires skilled staff and good data quality. Supported judgement: Usually worthwhile once data from several systems must be analysed regularly; cloud warehouses reduce cost, but benefits depend on data quality and clear business questions. items.stem:
Case study context: Saigon Fresh, a supermarket chain in Hanoi, analyses loyalty-card transactions with association rules, forecasts stock with regression and runs an inventory system based on linked lists and stacks.
(a) Distinguish between asynchronous replication and synchronous replication. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [2]
(b) Evaluate the claim that a global e-commerce company should use a distributed rather than a centralised database. Refer to Saigon Fresh in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Synchronous replication confirms a write only when all replicas are updated (consistent but slower); asynchronous confirms immediately and updates replicas later (faster but replicas may lag). (b) For a global company the availability and latency benefits usually outweigh the complexity, provided critical transactions use strong consistency.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Synchronous replication confirms a write only when all replicas are updated (consistent but slower); asynchronous confirms immediately and updates replicas later (faster but replicas may lag). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: lower latency for users worldwide; no single point of failure; scales by adding nodes; supports regional data-protection laws. Arguments against: more complex to design and administer; consistency across sites is harder (CAP trade-offs); distributed transactions are slower; higher network and security costs. Supported judgement: For a global company the availability and latency benefits usually outweigh the complexity, provided critical transactions use strong consistency. items.stem:
Case study context: Kente Market, an online craft marketplace in Accra, stores products as JSON documents, ranks listings with a neural network and processes orders through a queue-based service.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why a data lake can turn into a "data swamp". Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [2]
(b) "Organisations should store all their data in a data lake rather than a data warehouse." To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Because data is stored raw without enforced schema, poor metadata, cataloguing and governance make it hard to find, trust or understand the data, so it becomes unusable. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) Many organisations use both (or a "lakehouse"): the lake for raw and ML data, the warehouse for trusted reporting.

(b) [4 marks] Arguments for: cheap storage of any data type at scale; keeps raw data for future ML uses; fast ingestion with no up-front modelling. Arguments against: without governance it becomes a data swamp; business users need clean, structured data for reports; query performance and data quality are lower. Supported judgement: Many organisations use both (or a "lakehouse"): the lake for raw and ML data, the warehouse for trusted reporting.
